title: Sampling Distribution and p-Value Simulator
summary: Two groups of fictional participants are drawn from the same population, so the true difference is exactly zero. Running that study a thousand times builds the sampling distribution of the mean difference, and one observed difference is marked on it with the tails at least that far from zero shaded. The tail area counted in the pile is shown beside the tail area the model predicts. Sample size and variability can be changed, so the same observed difference can be watched moving from p = .5 to p below .001 without the finding changing at all.
learningObjectives: Describe a sampling distribution as the spread of a statistic across repeated studies under a stated model.
Read a p-value off a null distribution as a tail area rather than as a property of the data.
State what a p-value is not, including the probability that the null is true and the probability a result was due to chance.
Explain why the same observed difference yields different p-values at different sample sizes.
List the assumptions a reported p-value is conditional on.
privacy: No data collected, stored or transmitted; every study is generated in the browser tab, and the tool asks nothing about the person using it.
accessibilityNotes: Native ranges, a number input, checkboxes and buttons, each with an explicit label and grouped in a fieldset with a legend; every slider announces a meaningful value such as '40 participants in each group'. The histogram is hidden from assistive technology and paired inside its figure with a visible three-row table giving how many simulated studies fell below the negative observed value, between the two, and above the positive one, with shares. Tail bars carry a diagonal hatch as well as a different fill, and the observed value is marked with a labelled rule, so the tail area is never carried by colour alone. Four figures - standard error, the observed value in standard errors, the model's tail area and the counted tail area - sit beside the chart in the pinned block. p-values below .001 are reported as such rather than as a spurious third digit. Every run announces a full sentence through the polite live region, focus moves to the simulator heading when it opens, forced-colours rules are provided, and the layout is usable at 320px and at classroom-projector widths with the pinned block fitting inside a 768px-tall viewport.
readmeTopic: What a null world looks like: the sampling distribution, the tail area, and everything a p-value is not
simulationNotes: Two groups of n fictional participants are drawn from Normal(0, sigma), so the true difference is exactly zero and the statistic is the difference between the group means. The standard error is sigma times the square root of 2/n and the reference distribution is Normal(0, SE). The reference is normal rather than t because the null model states the population standard deviation, so nothing is estimated from the sample; a real t-test estimates it and pays with heavier tails, which is a later tool in this module and the page says so. The theoretical tail area is twice one minus the standard normal cumulative function of the observed value over the standard error, computed with the Abramowitz and Stegun 26.2.17 approximation; the simulated tail area is a count of how many generated studies reached at least that far from zero, and the two are shown side by side. Randomness is seeded with mulberry32 and Box-Muller normals, and changing the model clears the pile because those studies came from a different null world. Nothing in the tool mentions a 0.05 threshold, because whether a tail area of a given size should change anybody's behaviour is a decision rather than a statistical fact. No real study, participant or dataset is involved.
